title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-290-816-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-290-816-001 & 5-308-188-001
Issues
Whether the C3 – C4 ACDF surgery recommended by Dr. Hammers is
⮚
reasonable, necessary and related to the work injury of September 9, 2024
and/or the work injury of September 12, 2024?
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant is employed as a Pueblo Police Officer and has been employed by the
Pueblo Police department for over 15 years.
2. Claimant testified that on September 9, 2024, he was pursuing a suspect on foot
who he believed had been shoplifting. The suspect ran from Claimant and
Claimant ran after the suspect. As Claimant approached the suspect, while
running, Claimant pushed the suspect forward and “my head whipped backwards
and I felt, like, a burning and, like, tingling sensation down my arms”. After this
accident, Claimant’s supervisor asked if he was alright/not injured, to which
Claimant responded, “You know actually, I kind of tweaked my neck a little bit if
I’m being completely honest.”
3. A second incident occurred a few days later on September 12, 2024. Claimant
testified, “So very similar action from me, contacted a male, he ended up running.
When I caught up to him, I, again just trying to shove him down to the ground so
he wouldn’t keep running across the street. And as I went to shove him, I
pushed forward. He was a much larger male, so I pushed harder, but my head
went back harder because of that, and because of that neck whip, same thing,
but this time, it was extremely worse. It was burning, tingling, and it went from
my head down to my toes.”
1

4. Claimant testified that in 2012, while in the course and scope of employment
working as a Police Officer for the Pueblo Police Department, he experienced a
“much more subtle” incident to his neck, and he didn’t report it. Claimant testified
that he received no medical treatment after this incident and the symptoms
resolved “within a day or two.”
5. Another prior incident occurred in 2015 while working when he experienced a
“very similar incident to the previous one” regarding the neck. Claimant was seen
one time at Parkview Hospital after this incident but no other medical treatment
was received. Claimant’s symptoms resolved completely “after a week or two”.
6. Claimant credibly testified that he had no cervical spine pain from 2015 until the
two incidents in September, 2024. Nor did Claimant have any physical
restrictions prior to the two incidents.
7. Currently, Claimant’s symptoms include burning and tingling in his arm and
occasionally into his lower extremities.
8. Claimant testified on cross-examination that he’s “limited” now after the
September of 2024 accidents when he wears his SWAT gear. Regarding
wearing SWAT gear after these accidents, Claimant testified, “I notice the
pressure on my neck and my head more from the helmet on that. So, it definitely
kind of limits me on that”.
9. Dr. Hammers was asked to examine Claimant by Dr. Centi, the Authorized
Treating Physician (ATP), as there was concern for neurologic injury that might
require surgery. Dr. Hammers is Board Certified expert in neurosurgery. Dr.
Hammers testified that he reviewed the body cam footage from both dates of
accident and reviewed all of the medical records contained in Claimant’s medical
file.
10. Dr. Hammers diagnosed Claimant with cervical spondylosis and more
specifically, central cord syndrome and testified that his review of the body cam
footage/mechanism of injury, support this diagnosis. Dr. Hammers testified that
2

the 9/27/24 cervical MRI supports his diagnosis of central cord syndrome. Dr.
Hammers testified that the “cord edema” and what he called “spinal cord signal
change at C3-4” found on the 9/27/24 cervical MRI supports the fact that acute
injuries occurred on 9/9/24 and/or 9/12/24. Dr. Hammers testified that the spinal
cord bruise seen on the 9/27/24 cervical MRI was more likely than not, caused by
the 9/9/24 and/or 9/12/24 dates of accident.
11. Dr. Hammers has recommended an Anterior Cervical Discectomy Fusion surgery
at C3 – C4. Dr. Hammers testified that his request for the C3-C4 ACDF surgery
is reasonable, necessary, and related in order to cure or relieve the effects of the
workplace injury. He elaborated, “Central cord syndrome is a serious form of
spinal cord injury. It is commonly sustained by way of cervical spine injury, often
hyperextension injury. This is consistent with the suspected mechanism of injury.
The spectrum of potential symptoms from central cord syndrome is broad and
can range from minimal symptoms to paralysis. Proper treatment is surgery to
assist in the relief and recovery of symptoms and prevent future worsening.”
12. Dr. Centi, the authorized treating physician, agreed with Dr. Hammers that the
proposed surgery is reasonable, necessary and related to the work-place
injuries. Dr. Rook, who performed an IME at the request of the Claimant, agrees
with Dr. Centi and Dr. Hammers that the proposed surgery is reasonable,
necessary and related.
13. Respondents requested an IME with Dr. Mathwich. Dr. Mathwich testified that the
surgery requested by Dr. Hammers is “absolutely” reasonable to perform. Dr.
Hammers testified that, “The surgery absolutely needs to take place, and sooner
rather than later.” However, Dr. Mathwich does not believe that the requested
surgery is related to the work place accidents of 9/9/24 and/or 9/12/24.
3

Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S. is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law
judge. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637
(Colo. App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a
contrary inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make
credibility determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at
641. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions;
the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has
been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Ins. Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert
testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is
subject to conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting
4

part or none of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n,
441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
D. I am persuaded by the opinions of Dr. Hammers that the greatest likelihood that
the current injuries sustained in September of ’24 are the reason he is
symptomatic and requires surgery. This opinion is supported by the ATP and Dr.
Rook.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Respondents are liable for the ACDF surgery recommended by Dr. Hammers as
reasonable, necessary and related to the two work-related incidents in
September, 2024.
2. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
NOTE: If you are dissatisfied with the ALJ's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on the certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the ALJ's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it
within twenty (20) days after mailing or service of the order of the ALJ; and (2) That you
mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. You may
file your Petition to Review electronically by emailing the Petition to Review to the
following email address: oac-ptr@state.co.us. If the Petition to Review is emailed to the
aforementioned email address, the Petition to Review is deemed filed in Denver
5

pursuant to OACRP 27 and Section 8-43-301, C.R.S. If the Petition to Review is filed
by email to the proper email address, it does not need to be mailed to the Denver Office
of Administrative Courts. For further information regarding procedures to follow when
filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may access a petition to review
form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.
